function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a complete “starter kit” you can drop into the **zelarhq/nodejs‑welcome** repository.  
It contains:

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a lightweight Node.js image for the app |
| `k8s.yaml` | Deployment + Service (LoadBalancer) for Kubernetes |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | GitHub Actions pipeline that builds & pushes the image on every push to `main` |

---

## 1️⃣ Dockerfile

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
# ------------------------------------
# Base image – Alpine gives a small footprint
FROM node:18-alpine

# Working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /app

# Copy dependency descriptors first (optimises caching)
COPY package*.json ./

# Install production dependencies only
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port your app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Default command
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this image?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is the latest LTS Node image with a minimal size (~70 MB).  
> * `npm ci` guarantees a clean install from `package-lock.json`.  
> * The container listens on port **3000** – adjust if your app uses a different port.

---

## 2️⃣ Kubernetes YAML (`k8s.yaml`)

```yaml
# k8s.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **What this does**  
> * Deploys **2 replicas** of the pod.  
> * Exposes the app on port **80** externally, mapping to container port **3000**.  
> * Uses a **LoadBalancer** service – suitable for cloud providers that support external LB IPs.

---

## 3️⃣ GitHub Actions Workflow (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`)

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3

      # Set up Node.js
      - name: Set up Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v3
        with:
          node-version: '18'

      # Install dependencies
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      # Run tests (optional – remove if no tests)
      - name: Run tests
        run: npm test

      # Build Docker image
      - name: Build Docker image
        run: |
          docker build -t zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} .

      # Log in to Docker Hub (or any registry)
      - name: Log in to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v2
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_PASSWORD }}

      # Push image to registry
      - name: Push image
        run: docker push zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
```

> **Key points**  
> * The image is tagged with the commit SHA (`${{ github.sha }}`) – this gives you immutable, traceable images.  
> * Secrets `DOCKER_USERNAME` & `DOCKER_PASSWORD` must be added in the repo’s Settings → Secrets → Actions.  
> * If you don’t have tests, you can delete the “Run tests” step.

---

## 4️⃣ Add, Commit & Push

```bash
# From the root of the repo
git add Dockerfile k8s.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes YAML, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> **Tip** – If you’re on a different branch, replace `main` with your branch name.

---

### 🎉 Done!

Once pushed, GitHub Actions will automatically build the Docker image and push it to Docker Hub (or your chosen registry).  
The Kubernetes YAML can be applied with:

```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s.yaml
```

Feel free to tweak the image name, tags, replica count, or service type to suit your environment. Happy coding!
